lines.note: Ta completes prata from the preceding page. Ginzan teppeki compares exceptional strength to a silver mountain and iron wall; the second word reads teppeqi, not OCR toppeqi.

runs.text: ſima como ſerra de prata, & parede de ferro.

lines.note: Completes fortissima and translates the comparison as very strong, like a silver mountain range and iron wall. This is still the Guinzan entry begun on f238.
Gyoo means practices or virtuous works, explained by okonai. A faint final i survives in Voconai; vir- begins virtude below.
Completes virtude and closes the moral-practice definition. The damaged beginning belongs to this short body continuation, not to a new headword.
A separate gyoo is work or an occupation, explained by shiwaza. Obra is read through the damaged b; ko wa chichi no begins the example about a son and his father.

runs.text: O filho herda, ou toma o of

lines.note: Gyoo wo tsugu completes the example: the son inherits or takes up his father's occupation. The particle is uo, not OCR ao; of continues below without a clearly printed hyphen.
Completes officio and restates the father's occupation or activity. Pay retains the historical spelling.
Gyooboo concerns a rule or practice of observance, explained through okonoo nori and okonai. The headword's two differently shaped vowel marks are preserved.

runs.text: & exercicios como de Quareſma, Somana ſan-

lines.note: The Portuguese compares these observances with practices of Lent and Holy Week. The final ſan- is physically divided from cta below.
Completes sancta in Somana sancta. This small continuation is a full body row and closes the comparison with Christian observances.
Gyoobu concerns walking, explained by yuki and ayumu. To- begins toshiyotte, the age-related example on the following line.
Toshiyotte gyobu ga kanawanu says that advanced age prevents walking. The printed guiobuga has no extra a between bu and ga; its unaccented o is not regularized from the headword.
Completes velho: being old, I cannot walk. The Portuguese first-person interpretation supplies the subject omitted in Japanese.
Gyobutsu denotes fish, with uo as the Japanese equivalent. The scan supports Peixe and the headword Guiobut, correcting two OCR initial-letter errors.
Gyoka is a fisherman's house, paraphrased as sunadori iye. Preserve that printed paraphrase without supplying an unprinted no; S. marks written usage.

runs.text: Guioca. Von itoma. i, Von fima.

lines.note: Another gyoka denotes an honoured person's leisure or free time. On itoma and on hima are honorific equivalents; Tem- starts tempo below.

runs.text: po, ou deſocupação, falando de peßoa honra-

lines.note: The free time belongs to a person spoken of respectfully. The social qualification is part of the original gloss, not an added inference about the person.
Completes honrada and ends the written-register leisure entry. The brief line is separate from the following homograph about transport.
This gyoka is an honoured person's conveyance, explained by on norimono. Andas indicates a carrying chair or litter in the Portuguese gloss.
Honrada completes the respectful qualification of the person whose litter is described. It closes the third Guioca entry.

runs.text: A gradarſe o ſenhor do criado de

lines.note: Gyokan denotes a lord's pleasure or approval concerning a servant or something done. The conspicuous space after capital A is retained; the Portuguese construction continues below.
The gloss extends to approving or praising something. Gyokan nasaruru is the honorific example, divided after na-.
Completes nasaruru, the respectful verb used with gyokan. This single-word continuation remains a physical body line.
A different gyokan is a fishing rod, paraphrased as sunadori sao. The long s in ſauo is visible and is not an f.
The rod or cane belongs to a fisherman. This completes the fishing-implement sense before another separate homograph.

runs.text: Hũa iguaria de peixe cozido cõ cer-

lines.note: The next gyokan is a cooked fish dish with a particular seasoning. The initial is G rather than OCR C; cer- begins certa below.
Completes certa tempera, a specific seasoning or preparation. The definition provides no recipe, so none is inferred from the dish name.
Gyokkai is a staircase of costly stone. Preserve the doubled c and written-register label.
Gyokko is a precious jar or vessel, literally tama no tsubo. Boyão is the historical Portuguese vessel word, not a Japanese expression.
Crystal is given as an example of the vessel's material. This completes the preceding comparison without restricting the headword to crystal alone.
Gyokkotsu refers respectfully to bones, literally tama no hone. The gloss pairs a bone with skeletal remains and preserves its two different s representations.

runs.text: dalgum Rey morto, ou outra peßoa inſigne.

lines.note: The bones belong to a deceased king or another distinguished person. This qualification distinguishes the respectful usage from ordinary fish bones below.
Gyochoo combines fish and birds, explained by uo and tori. The circumflex and the paired Portuguese nouns are retained.
Gyokotsu here means fish bones, literally uo no hone. The single c distinguishes this entry graphically from Guioccot above.
Gyokkwoo is the radiance of precious stones, paraphrased as tama no hikari. The headword is one word; the OCR's Goio cquǒ introduced both a wrong vowel and a false boundary.
The gloss specifies precious stones, then begins an example in which their radiance lights the surroundings. Ca- continues into the verb on the next row.
Ca- plus cayacaſu gives kakayakasu as printed. The Portuguese identifies the radiance of the stones as the subject of the continuing statement.

runs.text: he tamanho que alumia ao derredor.

lines.note: The radiance is so great that it illuminates the surroundings. This completes the example without adding any unprinted intensifier to the Japanese.

runs.text: Esta palaura não ſe vſa ſe não compo

lines.note: Gyoku is said to occur only in combination with other words. Compo continues as composta below without a visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: ſta com outras, cujo vſo, & ſentido ſe verà a

lines.note: Completes composta and says the compounds' usage and sense will be shown below. The noun is vſo, not OCR vſa; the last a continues into the adverb a baixo.

runs.text: baixo nos vocabulos que della ſe compoem.

lines.note: The reader is directed to the following compounds formed from gyoku. The physical split a / baixo is preserved instead of combining the adverb editorially.
Gyokuban is a richly worked tray or table, literally tama no ban. Me continues into mesa below without an added hyphen; Bandeija retains the source's spelling.
Completes mesa and qualifies the object as richly worked and adorned. The wording need not imply that the entire object is made from a single gemstone.
Gyokuchuu is a precious pillar, explained by tama no hashira. The final u has a visible caron; pe- begins pedras below.

runs.text: dras precioſas, ou ornada de pedraria.

lines.note: The column is made of precious stones or adorned with them. Preserve the source's distinction between material and applied ornament.
The homographic gyokuchuu means inside a precious stone, as tama no uchi explains. It is distinct from the pillar entry despite identical romanization.
Completes the location within the precious stone. The scan supports precioſa with o rather than OCR precieſa.

zones.label: Column 2 running header
zones.note: V is printed in both running headers and is retained despite the Guioc- headwords.

lines.note: Gyokuko is a precious jar or vessel, again explained by tama no tsubo. The scan has Guiocuco without the OCR's extra i; it remains distinct from Guiocco in the other column.
The vessel is costly, for example made of crystal. The adjective rico qualifies the vessel rather than naming a separate material.
Gyokuden denotes richly ornamented royal palaces, paraphrased as tama no iye. Rica- begins the adverb ricamente below.
Completes ricamente and describes the palaces as richly worked and adorned. This closes the architectural definition.
Gyokudoo has the same palace meaning as Guiocuden. Idem refers to the immediately preceding entry and must not be expanded in the transcription.
Gyokuhaku is a letter or written sheet associated with a ruler, literally tama no kami. The following row specifies its author.
The letter or paper is written by the king. The historical expression el Rey and capital R are retained.
Gyokuhatsu is a costly basin, explained by tama no hachi. Preserve the final t of the historical reading rather than expanding it to modern tsu.
The basin is rich or precious. This one-word continuation closes Guiocufat.
Gyokuhoo is the ruler's face, with tama no kao and teioo no kao as Japanese paraphrases. The initial G corrects OCR C; the tight Tamanocauo is retained.
The Portuguese directly identifies the king's face. This belongs to the preceding headword rather than to the similar entry below.
Gyokugan is another respectful term for the ruler's face. Tama no kaobase introduces the feature; teioo no continues into the honorific phrase below.
On kao completes the honorific Japanese explanation. The repeated headword then begins an example involving respectfully seeing the ruler.
Gyokugan wo haishi-tatematsuru expresses respectfully beholding the ruler. The Portuguese has a visible word space in Ver ao Rey, not the baseline's Verao.
Gyokumon is an anatomical euphemism for female genitals. The opening Latin Os vuluæ refers to the vulval opening and uses a final ae ligature; the Portuguese explanation continues below.
Completes the reference to a woman's private parts and marks the term as written usage. The neutral anatomical gloss is retained without euphemistic rewriting.
Gyokukei is glossed in Latin as the male sexual organ. S. again marks written usage; the line is a complete independent entry.
Gyokuki denotes a precious stone's brilliance, explained by tama kagayaku as represented in the historical spelling. The gloss's object follows on the next row.
The radiance belongs to the precious stone. This completes Reſplandor rather than introducing a separate nominal entry.
Gyokukwa is glossed as a beautiful rose, with tama and hana as its Japanese components. Preserve the source's specific flower comparison rather than generalizing it to every flower.
The rose holds dew and has not yet opened: gyokukwa tsuyu wo fukunde imada hirakezu. The final fi continues below without a visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: A roſa que eſtà em botão ſem abrir

lines.note: Raqezu completes hirakezu, not yet open. The Portuguese describes the rose still in bud; its grave accent in eſtà is retained.
The unopened rose is covered in dew. S. marks the example as written usage.
Gyokukwan is a ring set with precious stones, literally tama no yubigane. The Portuguese's nasal abbreviation cõ continues its specification below.
The ring is furnished with precious stones. This completes Anel cõ and closes the jewellery entry.
Gyokuren denotes precious or richly decorated blinds, explained by tama no sudare. Pe continues as pedras without an added hyphen at the edge.

runs.text: dras precioſas. i, Ricas, & bem ornadas.

lines.note: The gloss explains the costly-stone description as rich and well adorned. This qualification should be preserved rather than insisting on a wholly literal gemstone construction.
A separate gyokuren is a rich carriage or litter, paraphrased as tama no teguruma. An continues into andas on the next physical row without a printed hyphen.
Completes andas and supplies carro as the alternative conveyance. This closes the transport homograph, distinct from the blinds above.

Gyokuryoo is a richly represented dragon-like emblem, with tama no ryoo as its Japanese paraphrase. The Portuguese literally calls it a lagarto, lizard; that wording is retained rather than corrected to dragão.

runs.text: pintado, ou eſculpido que o Dairi tem por ar-

lines.note: The emblem is painted or sculpted and used by the Dairi. Dairi is a Japanese title within the Portuguese explanation; ar- begins armas below.
Completes armas and identifies the motif as an insignia on the ruler's possessions. This explains the emblematic function of the image described above.
Gyokurin is explained by two tama elements and glossed as precious stones. The damaged u in the headword is read as u, not the OCR's n; the repeated synonym is genuine.
Gyokuroo denotes rich buildings or palaces, explained through tama no yagura. Preserve the circumflex rather than matching the caron of nearby different entries.
The example describes being seated in sumptuous buildings or a golden palace. Qindenni and zaſu retain their joined particle and historical spelling.

runs.text: Eſtar em ricas pouſadas, ou paços. S.

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the example as being in rich lodgings or palaces. The final S. marks written usage.
Gyokusaku praises a marvellous work. The scan shows a colon and the spelling louuando; the explanation restricts the compliment to a particular kind of work below.
The praise is applied to a work of poetry. This completes the usage explanation and marks the term as literary.
Gyokutaku means working or polishing precious stones, explained by tama wo migaku. Pe- begins pedras on the following line.
The example compares falling snow with worked precious stones. Koosetsu gyokutaku ni begins the comparison and continues with nitari below.

runs.text: A neue que cae pareceſe com pedras

lines.note: Nitari completes the resemblance construction. The Portuguese explicitly identifies falling snow as what resembles the stones.
The stones are precious and well worked. This completes the visual comparison without introducing a second Japanese example.

Gyokutai is the royal person or body, explained by teioo no mi. The scan supports Guiocutai and the rounded u in Teiuǒno, unlike the v in Teivǒno higher in this column; neither is regularized. Peßoareal remains tightly joined.
The body is that of the king. This completes the respectful personal reference, distinct from the following musical instrument.
Gyokuteki is a richly worked flute, literally tama no fue. The historical Portuguese Frauta and abbreviated ricamẽ- are retained.
Completes ricamente laurada, richly worked. This closes the flute entry at its physical line break.
Gyokuto is a literary name for the moon. The Portuguese prints only Lũa; no unprinted explanation of the name's imagery is added to the transcription.

zones.label: Quire signature
zones.note: The final numeral is heavily inked but retains the curved top and low foot of 2.
